tip: 'Prefer X to Y' normally uses από (apo = from), not παρά (para): προτιμάω τις κωμωδίες από τα δράματα (protimao tis komodhies apo ta dhramata) – you prefer one 'from' the other.
A TV season is normally called a κύκλος (kiklos = cycle): τρεις κύκλους (tris kiklus) = three seasons.
Το αρχαίο της Επιδαύρου (to arkheo tis Epidhavru = the ancient one of Epidaurus) is no ruin – the 4th-century BC theater still hosts plays every summer.
Έπαιζαν (epezan) = 'they were performing' – the ongoing-past form. It puts you inside the unfolding show; a one-off report would use έπαιξαν (epeksan).
Σειρά (sira) is both 'row' and 'series': πρώτη σειρά (proti sira) = front row, but a TV show is also a σειρά (sira). Context decides which.
Ανέβασαν (anevasan) is literally 'they raised' – Greek raises a play onto the stage. The same verb ανεβάζω (anevazo) also uploads files.
Διάλειμμα (dhialima) = break/intermission – the same word covers a school recess.
Όρθιοι (orthii = standing) is an adjective agreeing with 'we', not an adverb: χειροκροτήσαμε όρθιοι (khirokrotisame orthii) = we applauded standing.
Το σκηνικό (to skiniko) is the set – the scenery. Η σκηνή (i skini) is the stage itself. Close relatives, different parts of the theater.
Έκθεση (ekthesi) = exhibition – the same word also means a school essay.
Πίνακας (pinakas) covers 'painting' and '(black)board': κάθε πίνακα (kathe pinaka) here means each painting, but in a classroom it's the board.
Πινακοθήκη (pinakothiki) = art gallery – by its roots, a case for paintings.
Photos come out in Greek: βγάζουμε φωτογραφίες (vghazume fotoghrafies) is literally 'we take out photos'. Παίρνω (perno = take) is the classic wrong-verb slip here.
Από όσο (apo oso) = 'than' when a full clause follows: πιο μικρός από όσο φανταζόμουν (pio mikros apo oso fantazomun).
Απαγορεύεται (apaghorevete) = it is forbidden – a no-subject form, standard on signs.
Με ταξιδεύει (me taksidhevi) = it carries me away – Greek uses 'travel' figuratively for what a book does to you.
Πήρα δανεικό (pira dhaniko) is literally 'I took (it) on loan' – the everyday way to borrow. The adjective δανεικό (dhaniko = lent) carries the borrowing; the verb is just 'take'.
Βιβλιοθήκη (vivliothiki) = both 'library' and 'bookcase' – context decides which.
Δυνατά (dhinata) means 'strongly' and 'loudly': διάβασα δυνατά (dhiavasa dhinata) = I read aloud, not I read hard. For sound, strong means loud.
Δοκίμια (dhokimia) are literary essays – reflective prose. A school essay is an έκθεση (ekthesi). Greek splits what English packs into one word.
Βιβλιοπωλείο (vivliopolio) = bookshop – βιβλίο (vivlio = book) plus the -πωλείο (-polio) ending that marks a shop.
Μού κίνησε το ενδιαφέρον (mu kinise to endhiaferon) is literally 'it moved the interest to me' – Greek sets interest in motion rather than sparking it.
Greek has no infinitive, so 'before sleeping' needs a full verb: πριν κοιμηθώ (prin kimitho) = literally 'before I sleep' – the 'I' stays inside the verb.
Emphatic 'its own' agrees like an adjective: τους δικούς της χορούς (tus dhikus tis khorus) – δικούς (dhikus) wears the same ending as χορούς (khorus).
Αγκαλιά (angalia = embrace) is a bare noun doing adverb work: χορεύαμε αγκαλιά (khorevame angalia) = we danced embrace-style – no 'in an' needed.
Καθυστέρησε (kathisterise) is the one-and-done past: the delay happened, complete. An ongoing 'was running late' would be καθυστερούσε (kathisteruse).
English adds 'got' for 'got lost'; Greek packs it into the verb: χάθηκε (khathike) = it got lost. The -θηκε (-thike) ending does the 'got' work.
Λόγω (logho) = 'because of', and the next noun takes the 'of' form: λόγω της κακοκαιρίας (logho tis kakokerias) = by reason of the bad weather.
Αν γίνεται (an yinete) is literally 'if it happens' – Greek's everyday 'if possible' softener for requests, with no word for 'possible' in it.
Plain από (apo) can't stand alone before a clause – 'than I expected' normally takes απ' ό,τι: απ' ό,τι περίμενα (ap' oti perimena).
